questiontext.text: In open addressing, where are the entries stored?

answer.text: Directly in the table array itself — one entry per slot

feedback.text: Correct — no external lists; every element lives in a table slot.

answer.text: In a linked list hanging off each bucket

feedback.text: That is separate chaining, not open addressing.

answer.text: In a separate overflow file on disk

feedback.text: Open addressing keeps everything inside the in-memory array.

answer.text: In a balanced tree indexed by hash value

feedback.text: No tree is used; slots are plain array cells.

generalfeedback.text: Open addressing stores all n entries inside the m-slot array, so it needs no external node structures.

questiontext.text: When a key hashes to an occupied slot in open addressing, what happens next?

answer.text: It probes a sequence of alternative slots until an empty one is found

feedback.text: Correct — linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing generate the probe sequence.

answer.text: It appends the key to a linked list at that slot

feedback.text: That is chaining, not probing.

answer.text: It immediately doubles the table before inserting

feedback.text: Resizing may happen later, but the immediate response to a collision is probing.

answer.text: It overwrites the existing entry

feedback.text: That would lose data; probing preserves both keys.

generalfeedback.text: Open addressing resolves collisions by probing: it examines a deterministic sequence of slots (linear, quadratic, or double hashing) until it finds a free cell.

answer.text: Primary clustering — long runs of filled slots that lengthen future probes

feedback.text: Correct — contiguous occupied blocks grow and merge, hurting performance.

answer.text: It cannot be implemented without extra pointers

feedback.text: Linear probing needs no pointers; it just steps to the next slot.

answer.text: It requires the table size to be prime for double hashing

feedback.text: That constraint relates to double hashing, not linear probing's clustering.

answer.text: It makes the load factor exceed 1

feedback.text: Open addressing keeps α < 1; clustering is about probe length, not α > 1.

generalfeedback.text: Linear probing steps one slot at a time, so occupied cells clump into long contiguous runs (primary clustering) that make later probe sequences longer.

questiontext.text: Why is double hashing often preferred over linear probing?

answer.text: A second hash function spreads probes out, reducing clustering

feedback.text: Correct — the step size varies per key, avoiding the long contiguous runs of linear probing.

answer.text: It removes the need to keep the load factor below 1

feedback.text: All open addressing keeps α < 1; the probe scheme does not change that.

answer.text: It converts the table into a chained structure

feedback.text: Double hashing is still open addressing; no chains are used.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for tombstones on deletion

feedback.text: Deletion still needs tombstones regardless of the probe scheme.

generalfeedback.text: Double hashing uses a second hash to compute the step, so different keys follow different probe sequences and primary clustering is largely avoided.

questiontext.text: In open addressing the load factor α = n/m must stay below 1, because every entry occupies a distinct slot and the table can fill up.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — you cannot store more items than slots, so α < 1.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Unlike chaining, open addressing has a hard capacity of m entries.

questiontext.text: Deleting from an open-addressing table can simply blank the slot, with no special marker needed.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Blanking a slot can break probe chains for other keys; a tombstone marker is required.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — deletion must leave a tombstone so later probes still traverse past the removed slot.

questiontext.text: The special "deleted" marker left in a slot so that probe sequences keep working after a removal is called a ______.

answer.text: tombstone

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: tombstone*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about open addressing are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Linear, quadratic, and double hashing are all probing schemes it can use

feedback.text: Yes — these are the standard probe-sequence strategies.

answer.text: Deletion typically leaves a tombstone marker in the slot

feedback.text: Yes — otherwise probe chains would break.

answer.text: The load factor can freely exceed 1

feedback.text: No — with one entry per slot, α < 1 always.

answer.text: Each slot holds a linked list of colliding keys

feedback.text: No — that is separate chaining; open addressing keeps one entry per slot.

generalfeedback.text: Open addressing probes (linear/quadratic/double) with α < 1 and uses tombstones on deletion; it does not chain lists or allow α > 1.
